prompt.context: Our client, Bell Computer Inc., is the second largest PC manufacturer, by unit sales, in the United States. Over the past 5 years, Bell has been gaining market share and growing revenue, but at the same time, their net income is eroding. The founder of Bell has returned to the company and taken over as CEO. He has hired us to help.
prompt.question: Why have Bell's profit margins declined, and what can Bell do to improve its profitability and reach its 'Full Potential'?

clarifying_info.a: ASP stands for Average Selling Price — the average price at which the company sells a computer. Revenue equals units sold multiplied by ASP.
Assume only hardware is sold, as shown in the exhibits. Selling additional items (printers, software, warranties, etc.) could be explored as an improvement idea.

clarifying_info.q: Is this a domestic or international decision?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international operations.
'Full Potential' profitability can be interpreted as market-leading profitability.
'Client' refers to PCs designed for and sold to retail consumers, either directly or through a retailer like Best Buy.

clarifying_info.q: Do all competitors face the same pricing environment?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. All competitors face the same ASPs and sell comparable products.

exhibits.title: Product Mix breakdown by Business Segment for 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: Two pie charts showing PC units (in thousands) sold in 2005 and 2010, broken down by product type (Desktop, Laptop, Netbook) and by customer segment (Consumer, Corporate, Government). A note states that Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005 and that 'Other' products include Pocket PCs and Calculators.
exhibits.data: Unit mix across Desktop, Laptop, and Netbook categories for 2005 vs. 2010; Consumer, Corporate, and Government segment splits

exhibits.title: ASPs by Business Segment 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Average Selling Prices (ASPs) by PC product segment (Desktop, Laptop, Netbook) for 2005 and 2010. A note states that Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005.
exhibits.data: ASP figures by product type for 2005 and 2010; Laptop ASP declined from $2,000 (2005) to $750 (2010)

exhibits.title: Cost breakdown by competitor and cost category
exhibits.shows: A table showing cost per unit (or as a percentage) broken down by cost line (Parts/Components, Direct Labor, G&A, Marketing) for Bell and its key competitors (Haysus, Racer, HC) for 2010.
exhibits.data: Bell 2010 cost per unit breakdown; competitor benchmarks: Haysus parts cost ~$200, Racer direct labor ~$50, HC G&A ~$50, Bell marketing ~$50

framework: Revenue analysis: decompose into Units Sold x ASP across product segments (Desktop, Laptop, Netbook) and customer segments (Consumer, Corporate, Government) for 2005 vs. 2010
Cost analysis: decompose into Variable Costs per unit (parts, labor, marketing) and Fixed Costs (G&A/overhead) for 2005 vs. 2010
Profit per unit = ASP - Variable Cost/Unit - Fixed Cost/Unit; identify where the gap opened
Competitive benchmarking: compare Bell's cost structure line-by-line against best-in-class competitors to find 'Full Potential' cost savings
Revenue improvement levers: product mix management, pricing, new adjacent revenue streams
Cost reduction levers: procurement, labor, overhead, SKU rationalization

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what does the product mix shift tell us about Bell's revenue trajectory?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that consumer preference has shifted toward Laptops and that a new low-price segment (Netbooks) has emerged. Desktops have declined in share. This mix shift pushes blended ASP downward even before individual segment price declines.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what has happened to pricing and how does this affect revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that Laptop ASPs dropped sharply from $2,000 to $750 between 2005 and 2010. Combined with the mix shift toward Laptops (and the existence of low-ASP Netbooks), blended revenue per unit has fallen significantly. More units are sold but at much lower prices.

questions.prompt: Calculate Bell's net income (NI) from Laptops in 2005 vs. 2010 and quantify the decline.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute Revenue, Total Cost, and NI for both years using units sold, ASP, and cost per unit. The cost per unit remained flat at $800 while ASP fell from $2,000 to $750 — flipping from a $1,200 contribution to a -$50 loss per unit.

math.setup: NI = (ASP - Cost/Unit) x Units Sold. In 2005: ASP=$2,000, Cost/Unit=$800, Units=10K. In 2010: ASP=$750, Cost/Unit=$800, Units=30K.
math.answer: Laptop NI fell from +$12M (60% margin) in 2005 to -$1.5M (-6.7% margin) in 2010, a $13.5M deterioration, driven entirely by the ASP decline while costs stayed flat.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what is Bell's 'Full Potential' cost per unit for Laptops if it benchmarks against best-in-class competitors?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read each cost line and identify the lowest competitor cost in each category. Summing them gives a 'Full Potential' cost per unit. The reduction versus Bell's current $800/unit represents the achievable savings.

math.setup: Bell current cost/unit = $800. Best-in-class benchmarks: Parts = $200 (Haysus), Direct Labor = $50 (Racer), G&A = $50 (HC), Marketing = $50 (Bell, already at best). Full Potential cost = sum of best-in-class costs.
steps: Full Potential NI = (ASP - Full Potential Cost) x Units = ($750 - $350) x 30K
math.answer: Full Potential cost/unit = $350 (saving $450/unit). Full Potential Laptop NI = $12.0M (53.3% margin), a $13.5M improvement vs. 2010.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the cost benchmarking identified in Exhibit 3, what other ways could Bell improve its profitability?

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Sell complementary high-margin products: printers, software licenses, accessories
Offer extended warranties and service contracts
Expand into higher-margin corporate/government segments which may be less price-sensitive
Introduce a premium product line with higher ASPs

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: SKU rationalization — reduce the number of product models to lower complexity and procurement costs
Consolidate supplier base to improve parts pricing leverage
Offshore or automate direct labor further
Renegotiate G&A contracts and reduce overhead
Improve supply chain efficiency to reduce inventory carrying costs

categories.name: Strategic / competitive moves
ideas: Form strategic partnerships or JVs for component procurement
License technology to reduce R&D duplication
Explore M&A of a lower-cost manufacturer
Shift product mix further toward higher-margin segments (e.g., commercial PCs, servers)

recommendation: Bell's margin erosion is driven by a sharp decline in Laptop ASPs (from $2,000 to $750) combined with flat cost structures, in the context of a consumer mix shift toward Laptops and Netbooks.

Bell should immediately pursue cost reduction by benchmarking against best-in-class competitors: adopting Haysus's parts procurement ($200/unit), Racer's direct labor model ($50/unit), and HC's G&A structure ($50/unit), which would reduce cost/unit by $450 and restore Laptop NI to $12.0M at a 53.3% margin.
risks: Competitors may continue to reduce ASPs, eroding the margin recovery
Best-in-class cost benchmarks may require significant operational changes (supplier renegotiation, labor restructuring) that take time and carry execution risk
Netbook segment growth could further pressure blended ASPs if Bell does not manage product mix
Cost reduction programs could affect product quality or customer satisfaction
next_steps: Engage Haysus, Racer, and HC to understand the specific procurement and operational practices driving their cost advantages
Develop a phased implementation roadmap for cost reduction across parts, labor, and G&A
Evaluate SKU rationalization opportunities to reduce complexity
Assess adjacency revenue streams (warranties, software, accessories) to supplement hardware margins
